items.prompt: Define industrialisation.
items.canonical_answer: Industrialisation is growth in the importance and capacity of industrial production within an economy.
marking_guidance: Meaning: growing importance and capacity of industrial production within an economy.

items.prompt: Explain why new industrial equipment alone may not produce the expected output.
items.canonical_answer: Equipment needs suitable inputs, operation and maintenance. If any necessary support is absent, installed capacity may remain unused rather than becoming useful production.

items.prompt: Describe the production relationship in this fictional factory: cutting stays at 100 sets a day; stitching and completed output rise from 60 to 90 sets; the daily unfinished queue growth falls from 40 to 10 sets.
items.canonical_answer: Reducing the imbalance between stages accompanies higher completed output. Stitching rises by 30 sets, while queue growth falls by 30, with cutting unchanged.
marking_guidance: Evidence: accurately use the output and backlog changes.
Relationship: link better-balanced stages with more useful finished output; faster cutting is not the change shown.

items.prompt: Explain why naming land, labour and capital does not by itself answer a question about industrial infrastructure.
items.canonical_answer: Those are factor-of-production categories, whereas infrastructure refers to supporting networks and services such as roads, electricity and communications. Test whether the question asks about inputs or their supporting connections; a produced road can have both a capital-asset role and an infrastructure role.
marking_guidance: Error: the input classification substitutes for the requested network/service description.
Distinction: supporting systems versus factor categories, without claiming there can be no overlap.
Original indicative practice guidance; not an official mark scheme.

items.prompt: Differentiate between import substitution and export-orientated industrialisation.
items.canonical_answer: Import substitution develops domestic production to replace imports; export-orientated industrialisation develops production primarily for foreign markets.

items.prompt: Explain which strategy better fits a fictional district’s immediate aim of reliable local work. Small domestic production can meet steady local bag demand with available skills. A proposed large export plant has prospective buyers but lacks finance and a workable shipping route. Weigh both options.
items.canonical_answer: The smaller domestic operation is better supported now because demand and capabilities are available. The export plant offers a potentially larger market but lacks two necessary means to serve it, making its promised work less feasible. It could be reconsidered if finance and shipping are secured.
marking_guidance: Judgement: choose against reliable near-term work.
Reason: weigh feasible local demand against the export capacity constraints; accept a conditional alternative that addresses both gaps.
Original indicative practice guidance; not an official mark scheme.

items.prompt: Explain the error in calling one occasional sale of surplus goods abroad proof of export-orientated industrialisation.
items.canonical_answer: An export is a sale abroad; export-orientated industrialisation is a strategy developing productive capacity primarily for foreign markets. Test whether the evidence shows a planned production direction rather than a single transaction.
marking_guidance: Error: one foreign sale substitutes for an industrial strategy.
Distinction: transaction versus productive-market strategy, with the direction-of-production test.

items.prompt: Explain whether import substitution suits this fictional case: a local producer can match imported school-bag quality, has reliable inputs and steady local orders, but its unit cost is slightly higher. The aim is to build local capacity without making bags unaffordable.
items.canonical_answer: It is plausible because inputs, quality and demand support productive learning and local work. The higher cost could undermine affordability, so suitability depends on keeping the price within users’ means or reducing costs as capacity develops. Domestic production alone does not settle the combined aim.
marking_guidance: Judgement: supported conditional suitability against capacity and affordability.
Reason: weigh the demand/input strengths with the higher cost; an unconditional claim of self-sufficiency is insufficient.
Original indicative practice guidance; not an official mark scheme.

items.prompt: Explain whether a fictional producer should expand for confirmed foreign orders when quality and equipment are suitable but the delivery route is unreliable. Its aim is dependable export earnings.
items.canonical_answer: Expansion should depend on securing a reliable delivery arrangement. Confirmed demand and suitable capacity favour exporting, but failed delivery can prevent earnings and damage future orders. A staged expansion after resolving transport is better supported than treating foreign demand alone as enough.
marking_guidance: Judgement: decide against dependable earnings.
Reason: weigh the actual capacity and orders against the route constraint.
Original indicative practice guidance; not an official mark scheme.

items.prompt: Explain which scale suits an invented repair group with small varied orders, skilled hand workers and little investment finance: a flexible small workshop or a large automated line needing high-volume standardised sales.

Reason: weigh flexibility and existing resources against the line’s demand and finance requirements.

items.prompt: Explain whether a fictional multinational proposal meets a district’s aim of local skill development: it finances equipment and 80 jobs, but offers no training and imports its specialist team. A smaller alternative funds 40 jobs with documented local training.
items.canonical_answer: The smaller alternative is more directly aligned with the skill aim because it includes a training route. The multinational offers more jobs and finance, but its specialist arrangement supplies no evidence of local skill transfer. It may fit better if credible training commitments are added; job numbers alone do not establish the stated outcome.
marking_guidance: Judgement: relate the choice to skills rather than jobs alone.
Reason: weigh the larger employment offer against actual training provision and retained capability.

items.prompt: Explain whether an invented local processor should use a joint venture. It has buyers and local knowledge but insufficient equipment finance; a partner offers finance and training with clear shared-control terms. The alternative is a smaller operation it can fund alone. The aim is increased output with local participation.
items.canonical_answer: The joint venture is supported if the agreed terms can be implemented: it addresses missing finance while retaining local involvement and adding training. Independent operation preserves sole control but limits feasible capacity. The terms, rather than the partner’s nationality alone, make the proposed gain credible.
marking_guidance: Judgement: choose against output and local participation.
Reason: weigh the finance/training and control arrangements against the smaller feasible independent option.
Original indicative practice guidance; not an official mark scheme.

items.prompt: Explain which option better fits affordable service to sparsely served communities: a fictional state enterprise has funded maintenance and an access obligation; a private alternative promises faster expansion but has no provision for low-income users.
items.canonical_answer: The state option better matches affordable access under the supplied arrangements. The private proposal’s faster expansion is a benefit, but it does not address the specified users unless workable access protection is added. State ownership itself is not the reason: funded maintenance and the access arrangement are decisive.
marking_guidance: Judgement: compare the same affordable-access aim.
Reason: weigh speed against funded delivery and access provisions; avoid claiming state ownership guarantees performance.

items.prompt: Explain whether a fictional public private partnership is preferable to direct public provision for a processing site. It provides equipment finance sooner but its contract requires payment to the private partner even if equipment fails; direct provision is slower but has funded maintenance. The aim is dependable useful capacity within a limited public budget.
items.canonical_answer: The partnership’s speed is attractive but its failure-payment term exposes the limited public budget without assuring useful capacity. Direct provision is better supported unless the partnership can allocate performance responsibility and maintenance more credibly. Compare the actual risk and delivery terms rather than assuming a partnership removes public costs.
marking_guidance: Judgement: decide against dependable capacity and the budget constraint.
Reason: weigh financing speed against failure risk and maintenance; a supported renegotiation condition is valid.
Original indicative practice guidance; not an official mark scheme.

Its value depends on effective repair and maintenance, rather than expenditure alone.

items.prompt: Explain the productive change in an invented processor: the same 100 input units yield 70 saleable and 30 spoiled before a handling change, then 90 saleable and 10 spoiled after it.
items.canonical_answer: Saleable output rises by 20 while spoilage falls by 20 from unchanged input. Reduced loss allows more useful product without additional raw-material use, although the before-and-after data alone does not isolate the handling change from other possible causes.
marking_guidance: Mechanism: connect lower loss to the input-to-saleable conversion.
Consequence: more useful output without higher extraction, supported by the paired figures.

items.prompt: State (a) what is meant by division of labour and coordination of tasks [2]. Explain (b) the productive priority in an invented factory where cutting completes 120 sets daily but stitching completes 70 and the unfinished queue grows daily. Buyers want completed items and extra cutting capacity is proposed [4].
items.canonical_answer: (a) Division of labour allocates specialised tasks to different workers; coordination links the timing and flow between them. (b) Stitching is the constrained stage: 50 more sets are cut than stitched daily. Extra cutting would increase unfinished work rather than completed items. Improving or matching flow to stitching capacity addresses useful output for the buyers more directly.
marking_guidance: Point (a), 2 marks: correct meanings for task allocation and linking task flow.
Development (b), up to 4 marks: use the stage imbalance and buyer requirement to explain the bottleneck and why extra cutting is weaker.
Original indicative practice guidance; not an official mark scheme.

items.prompt: Describe (a) the relationship in this original fictional comparison, with the same raw input and quality standard: Process A uses 100 input units, gives 60 saleable units and 40 spoiled; B uses 100, gives 85 saleable and 15 spoiled [3]. Suggest (b) which process an industrial group should adopt to increase useful output without more extraction; staff and maintenance for either are available [3].
items.canonical_answer: (a) B combines 25 more saleable units with 25 fewer spoiled units from the same input. Lower loss accompanies greater useful output. (b) B fits the aim because it improves conversion of existing material while avoiding additional extraction. The stated skills and maintenance make adoption feasible under these facts; no unprovided price saving is assumed.
marking_guidance: Evidence (a), up to 3 marks: pair the output and spoilage differences for unchanged input.
Meaning (b), up to 3 marks: choose against useful output/resource use and justify with data and support conditions.
Original indicative practice guidance; not an official mark scheme.
